il_jackson_falls_2.blurb:
Jackson Falls is the best-known climbing area in southern Illinois: a run of sandstone bluffs and boulders tucked into a wooded hollow of the Shawnee National Forest near Ozark. Dozens of separate walls hold several hundred named lines, most of them bolted sport routes of fifty to sixty feet, with a smaller scattering of trad lines and boulder problems.

The sandstone is grippy and the grades feel stout; relatively few routes sit below 5.10, so the easier climbs get crowded on busy weekends. It suits intermediate and advanced sport climbers who want steady, friction-style face climbing in a shaded forest. Ticks are common in the warm months and there is no cell service in the hollow.
il_jackson_falls_2.parking_note: From Ozark, follow Ozark Road east, then Trigg Tower Road and Falls Road onto the dirt and gravel forest road. Park in the pull-offs about two miles in, just before and after the creek crossing. The road turns slick and has several creek crossings, so high clearance helps after rain.
il_jackson_falls_2.approach: From the pull-offs a trail drops steeply through the woods to the bluffs, a scramble of five to ten minutes. The slopes and the stream edge are slippery when wet.

tn_stone_fort_bouldering.blurb:
Stone Fort, also called Little Rock City, is a famed sandstone bouldering area in the woods beside the Montlake golf course near Soddy-Daisy, north of Chattanooga. Hundreds of problems are spread through a tight maze of blocks, corridors and walls, from easy warm-ups to some of the hardest lines in the Southeast.

The boulders sit close together, so walks between problems are short. It is a bouldering destination for every level, with good landings, mostly steep and powerful sandstone, and real crowds in the cool months.
tn_stone_fort_bouldering.parking_note: From Chattanooga take US-27 north, exit at Dayton Pike and turn left, then left onto Montlake Road and right onto Brow Lake Road. The clubhouse is about 0.2 miles along on the left; park in the marked climber parking and check in inside before heading to the boulders.
tn_stone_fort_bouldering.approach: From the clubhouse a short trail leads into the woods to the first boulders. Most of the area is compact and reached in a few minutes on foot.

ca_belvedere_heights_bouldering.blurb:
Belvedere Heights is a granite bouldering zone on the slopes of Box Springs Mountain, above Riverside in the Box Springs Mountain Reserve. More than a hundred boulders are scattered across the hillside, with problems from easy V0 up to about V5; technical slabs and long traverses are the main styles.

It is the most hike-heavy of the Box Springs bouldering areas, so it tends to be quiet. It suits local climbers wanting low-key sessions on rough granite, best in the cooler months when the Inland Empire sun is bearable.
ca_belvedere_heights_bouldering.approach: Trails from the Blaine Street end of the reserve branch toward the different boulder clusters. Walks run from about ten minutes to an hour depending on the zone, and the climbing is spread over a fairly steep slope.

tn_7_orange_blossom_wall.blurb:
Orange Blossom Wall is one of the numbered sectors along the Tennessee Wall, a roughly two-mile band of orange sandstone in the Prentice Cooper area northwest of Chattanooga. The sector carries well over a hundred lines of mostly traditional climbing, crack and face routes from 5.7 through the hard grades, with the bulk at 5.10 and 5.11.

The wall soaks up winter sun and is a favourite cold-season destination for Chattanooga climbers. It suits trad climbers comfortable placing their own gear on sandstone, and rewards a rack with plenty of small and medium cams and nuts.
tn_7_orange_blossom_wall.approach: The trail from the parking area reaches the wall in about thirty minutes, then runs along the base of the cliff to the numbered sector.

co_cactus_cliff.blurb:
Cactus Cliff is one of the main crags at Shelf Road, the limestone sport-climbing canyon north of Cañon City. It holds some of the longer lines in the canyon, with more than 150 bolted routes from 5.5 up to the low 5.14s and the bulk between 5.9 and 5.12, so there is something for a wide range of abilities.

The rock is pocketed, featured limestone, and the cliff is a good choice for climbers wanting sustained pitches. It draws steady crowds in spring and fall, and can be comfortable on sunny winter days too.

ar_north_forty_routes.blurb:
The North Forty is the largest and busiest wall at Horseshoe Canyon Ranch, a sandstone canyon in the Ozarks near Jasper. More than 160 routes line the cliff, most of them bolted with a solid share of trad lines, running from about 5.4 up to 5.13.

The bulk of the climbing is moderate, so it suits newer leaders and groups of mixed ability, while a good selection of 5.11 and low 5.12 lines keeps stronger climbers busy. Expect well-worn holds and crowds on weekends in the cooler months.
ar_north_forty_routes.approach: A short, easy walk of roughly ten minutes from the ranch's camping field follows the canyon trail to the base of the wall.

ut_wall_street.blurb:
Wall Street is a long, tall Wingate sandstone cliff band beside the Colorado River a few minutes west of Moab. Climbs begin almost at the roadside, which makes it one of the most convenient and popular crags in the area.

Routes span roughly 5.5 to 5.12 and beyond, with a deep supply of 5.10 and 5.11 lines on sustained vertical faces and cracks. Both sport and traditional climbing are on offer, and the crowds can be heavy on good-weather days. Passing traffic on the narrow road, trucks included, calls for care around parked cars and ropes.
ut_wall_street.approach: Almost none: most routes start within a few steps of the pull-outs along the road, with only a short scramble up the talus to the base.

or_spring_mountain.blurb:
Spring Mountain is a remote cliff at around 4,600 feet in the Blue Mountains of northeast Oregon, between Pendleton and La Grande. The rock is a solid, fine-grained volcanic stone close to basalt, with a long wall of face and crack climbing on varied features.

Most routes are bolted sport lines of about a hundred feet, from roughly 5.5 up to 5.12 with the greatest concentration from 5.9 to 5.11, alongside a good set of trad lines. It is a quiet spot for climbers happy to drive forest roads for uncrowded cragging among the pines.
or_spring_mountain.parking_note: From I-84 take exit 243 (Summit Road, Mount Emily), head north over the interstate and follow gravel FS-31 for about 8 miles. Turn left onto FS-3109 near the Whitman Route overlook sign, then after about a mile turn north onto the spur at a grassy meadow and follow it roughly half a mile to the boulder-blocked turnaround, which is the parking.
or_spring_mountain.approach: An easy trail leads from the road end to the base of the wall in five to seven minutes.

wy_nautilus_2.blurb:
The Nautilus is a distinctive granite formation at Vedauwoo, the rounded, boulder-strewn outcrop country between Laramie and Cheyenne. Its curled, shell-like roof gives it a recognisable profile, and it holds a large collection of routes on cracks and faces.

Climbing here is mostly traditional with a handful of bolted lines, and the rough Sherman granite rewards good crack technique. It is one of the most accessible formations at Vedauwoo thanks to a very short walk, so it works well for a quick session or as a warm-up before the area's harder offwidths.
wy_nautilus_2.parking_note: Drive past the main Vedauwoo campground turn-off to the next dirt lot on the left, the one with a restroom visible from the road. The Nautilus rises right beside it.
wy_nautilus_2.approach: A couple of minutes on foot from the dirt lot to the nearest climbs; routes around the far side of the formation take up to about ten minutes.
